forecasts.label: Capital financing requirement
forecasts.note: Restated at each quarterly return. The Q4 restatement comes from the annual return itself, so it lands on the outturn by construction — the interesting movement is Q1 to Q3.

forecasts.label: Interest payable
forecasts.note: The council's own full-year forecast, restated at each quarterly return.

forecasts.label: Revenue spending (net current expenditure)
forecasts.note: The full-year forecast of net current expenditure — the running cost of services — restated each quarter against the same measure at outturn.

forecasts.label: Capital expenditure
forecasts.note: Total capital spending forecast each quarter (the capital payments return) against the annual capital outturn. Capital spending not met from grants or receipts is what turns into new borrowing, so a forecast running ahead of outturn is a borrowing signal.

in_year.label: Interest payable, as reported each quarter
in_year.note: Per quarter, not cumulative. The quarterly return is a lighter collection than the annual one and sums to roughly 92% of it nationally, so the two are shown apart rather than added together.

news_drafts.headline: Hillingdon expects to use £83m of £88m exceptional support sought for 2025/26, £40m to restore reserve
news_drafts.lead:
Hillingdon Council expects to use £83m of the £88m of exceptional financial support it requested for 2025/26, the Audit, Finance & Performance Committee was told on 3 November. Exceptional financial support is government permission to borrow, or sell assets, to cover day-to-day spending. Of the £83m, £40m is to restore the General Fund reserve, according to the papers, which say 2025/26 accounts were closed on 6 August.

The council applied for the support and received an in-principle agreement in February 2026, before its budget was debated. The in-principle amounts agreed by government were £88m in 2025/26 and £62m in 2026/27, and the paper gives an in-principle figure of £173m across 2025/26 to 2027/28. It describes a later "minded to" award, says the associated costs have been accounted for, and says oversight requirements are still being defined.

The committee's governance paper puts the 2025/26 outturn at £7m better than the position projected in the second half of that year. It says that improvement has been used to reinvest in earmarked reserves depleted the previous year. The same paper says significant progress has been made but that "the Council is by no means out of the woods in restoring financial stability". It says delivering this year's budget, and a medium-term financial strategy that reduces and eliminates dependency on the support, will be key. A Best Value Notice dated 15 July 2026 sets out increased responsibilities for the new externally chaired Improvement and Assurance Board.

news_drafts.headline: Hillingdon reports a £50m budget gap as Cabinet is asked to consider higher fees and charges
news_drafts.lead:
Hillingdon Council has a current budget gap of £50m, according to a fees and charges report prepared for its Cabinet meeting on 22 October 2026. The report proposes increases to the charges the council makes for its services.

The report says that bringing in "some of the other increases before the end of the financial year will help the Council to reduce the reliance on Exceptional Financial Support in 2026/27". Exceptional financial support is government permission to borrow, or sell assets, to cover day-to-day spending, and is a last resort for councils.

The report is part of the papers for the Cabinet meeting. The extract available does not say which charges would rise, by how much, or how much each increase would raise.

news_drafts.headline: Hillingdon pension fund surplus hits £330m as investment returns lift funding to 124%
news_drafts.lead: Hillingdon's pension fund has swung to a surplus of £330m, up from £210m a year earlier, after delivering investment returns of 21.5% over 15 months to June. The fund's assets now cover 124% of its liabilities, up from 118%, meaning it has more than enough money to pay pensions promised to staff. The improvement means the fund needs annual investment returns of only 4.5% to stay fully funded, down from 5.1%, with a probability of 88% of achieving that target. Over five years, the fund has returned 6.7% annually, exactly matching its long-term objective, though it has underperformed its own benchmark by about 1% a year across all periods. The stronger short-term performance and improved funding position suggest recent strategy changes are beginning to take effect.

findings.paper_title: agenda item 8 - LG Reserve Risk Assessment Update Report
findings.headline: EY will seek a variation to its scale fee for the reserves risk assessment, the MHCLG submission and this report.
findings.detail: EY says these activities are outside the scope of the scale fee in its Audit Planning Report of 30 April 2026. The variation will go through the PSAA scale fee variation process, and EY will report the agreed costs later.
findings.matters: Additional audit fees created by a disclaimer and rebuild process are a cost other councils facing the same reset will also meet.
findings.quote: we will seek a variation to the scale fee

findings.paper_title: agenda item 8 - LG Reserve Risk Assessment Update Report
findings.headline: Assurance was obtained over the 31 March 2025 closing balances of Earmarked Reserves, the Dedicated Schools Grant Adjustment Account and the Pensions Reserve, so these need no rebuilding.
findings.detail: The dashboard rates these three reserves Lower Inherent Risk and states that assurance was obtained over their closing balances at 31 March 2025. EY notes that the rest of the lower-risk reserves may support a more targeted and proportionate rebuild, subject to audit evidence being available.
findings.matters: Earmarked reserves and the pensions reserve are the balances a lender or finance director would most want assured, and EY reports them as already assured to 31 March 2025.
findings.figures: Closing balance date: 31 March 2025 (no £ amounts stated)
findings.quote: Assurance was obtained over closing balances at 31 March 2025, so no rebuilding required

findings.paper_title: agenda item 8 - LG Reserve Risk Assessment Update Report
findings.headline: EY reports the capacity of Hillingdon's finance team and the quality of council information as significant weaknesses for 2024/25, and as risks of significant weakness for 2025/26.
findings.detail: EY links these two factors to the council's ability to support the external audit process. It says they were reported as significant weaknesses in the 2024/25 arrangements and carried into the Audit Planning Report as risks of significant weakness for 2025/26.
findings.matters: Finance team capacity and information quality are the stated reasons EY gives for not progressing the reserves rebuild, which other councils with similar staffing pressures would recognise.
findings.quote: were reported in our Audit Planning Report as risks of significant weakness for 2025/26

findings.paper_title: agenda item 8 - LG Reserve Risk Assessment Update Report
findings.headline: EY rates the General Fund as a significant risk of material misstatement among Hillingdon's usable reserves.
findings.detail: The dashboard places the General Fund in the Significant Risk category, defined as the cumulative balance of all income and expenditure less adjustments impacting other reserves. The Revaluation Reserve and Capital Adjustment Account are also rated Significant Risk, while the HRA and Capital Grants Unapplied Reserve are rated Higher Inherent Risk.
findings.matters: The General Fund is the council's main revenue reserve, so its risk rating goes directly to how far the council can rely on its stated balance.
findings.quote: General Fund (Usable) Significant Risk Cumulative balance of all income and expenditure less adjustments impacting other reserves

findings.paper_title: agenda item 8 - LG Reserve Risk Assessment Update Report
findings.headline: EY says Hillingdon's progress on rebuilding audit assurance falls behind the timescales in NAO guidance LARRIG 01.
findings.detail: EY's illustrative timetable under LARRIG 01 is compared with the council's actual position, which is shown as disclaimer in each year from 2023/24 to 2025/26. EY says that until the natural rebuild process can be supported, the historic gaps cannot be rebuilt. It asks the council to focus on high-quality financial statements and working papers for 2025/26.
findings.matters: Finance officers at other councils can compare their rebuild progress against the same LARRIG 01 timetable.
findings.quote: falls behind the expected timescales set out in LARRIG 01
